title: Short Stuff: Knock on Wood
summary: Short Stuff episode on knocking on wood and other good-luck and bad-luck-warding customs. Josh and Chuck trace knocking on wood to ancient Celtic beliefs about spirits in oak trees, then to a more recent British children's game, touch wood (tig touch wood), citing folklorist Steve Rowd and an 1891 book, The Boy's Modern Playmate. They discuss a 2013 University of Chicago study on physical action and luck, the Turkish ear-pull, Italian touch iron, Greek and Jewish spitting against the evil eye, Danish saving and throwing broken dishes at New Year's Eve, crossed fingers (an Oxford explanation tying it to early Christians is dismissed as unfounded, with the practice dated to 1912), and Chinese New Year house-cleaning customs. The episode closes with a Thai penis amulet (palad kiek) tradition.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the short episode on knocking on wood, noting it is about avoiding tempting fate rather than seeking good luck, and that people knock to ward off bad luck when boasting.

segments.title: Origins: Celts, touch wood, and luck studies
segments.summary: The hosts describe the ancient Celtic belief that oak trees held spirits, and competing explanations of knocking to wake spirits or drown out talk. They cite folklorist Steve Rowd tracing touch wood to an 1891 children's book and the British game tig touch wood. They also discuss a University of Chicago study from 2013 finding people felt luck worked when they took a physical action.

segments.title: Knock-on-wood variations: Turkey and Italy
segments.summary: Chuck mentions a Turkish practice of knocking twice and pulling an earlobe, and an Italian phrase, touch iron. Josh jokes that Italians have it wrong.

segments.title: Spitting against the evil eye
segments.summary: Josh describes Greek spitting three times to erase envy and the evil eye, which is also a practice in Jewish culture, and Chuck mentions spitting over the shoulder.

segments.title: Denmark's broken dishes
segments.summary: Chuck explains Danish people save broken dishes through the year and deliver them to friends or family on New Year's Eve as a wish for good luck, sometimes leaving a pile on a doorstep.

segments.title: Crossed fingers
segments.summary: Josh covers crossed fingers, the claim that early Christians originated it, and an Oxford article dating the gesture to 1912 and calling the Christian origin story unfounded. Chuck describes a double-crossed-fingers ritual with a friend.

segments.title: Chinese New Year house cleaning
segments.summary: Chuck describes sweeping dirt inward before Chinese New Year and avoiding sweeping out the front door to keep good luck. Josh says he adopted not cleaning for a few days after Western New Year.

segments.title: Thai penis amulet
segments.summary: Chuck describes the palad kiek, a small penis-shaped amulet that Thai men and boys wear in their pants for luck and possibly to lessen the severity of injury.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts exchange good-luck wishes and close the episode.
